subject: science
topic: Every cell in your body keeps time
angle: While the brain's SCN acts as a master pacemaker, nearly every cell in the body contains its own clock that can be independently adjusted by factors like metabolism and local signals.
title: The Federated Body Clock

hooks.text: Who is setting your internal pace?
You think your brain controls your time. Your cells disagree.
Your midnight meal is rewriting your cellular code.
A plate of food on a dark table.

reveal.headline: Your cells have their own clocks.
reveal.body: Circadian clocks exist in nearly every cell of your body, not just in your brain.

explain.headline: Local clocks operate independently.
explain.body: These clocks can be adjusted by metabolism and local signals. They act as gatekeepers that temporally adjust your cellular responses to external stimuli.

matters.headline: The brain is not the only master.
matters.body: Your body functions as a federated system. Local factors interact with systemic signals to regulate your rhythms.

example.headline: A meal at midnight.
example.body: Eating late at night shifts the phase of gene expression in your liver while your brain's master clock remains unaffected.

question.headline: Who is actually setting your pace?

stat.label: the amount of change in peripheral cell gene expression from feeding times

claims.text: A surprisingly small number of tissue rhythms are lost when only local clocks are ablated.
claims.quote: First, a surprisingly small number of tissue rhythms are lost when only local clocks are ablated

claims.text: Changing feeding times can change the phase of circadian gene expression in peripheral cell types by up to 12 h while leaving the SCN unaffected.
claims.quote: Here we show that temporal feeding restriction under light-dark or dark-dark conditions can change the phase of circadian gene expression in peripheral cell types by up to 12 h while leaving the phase of cyclic gene expression in the SCN unaffected.

claims.text: Peripheral clocks act as gatekeepers that temporally adjust cellular responses to external stimuli.
claims.quote: peripheral clocks controlling some local rhythms while at the same time acting as gatekeepers that temporally adjust cellular responses to external stimuli.

claims.text: Circadian clocks exist in nearly every body cell, not just in the brain's suprachiasmatic nucleus.
claims.quote: In mammals, the circadian timekeeping system has a complex architecture, composed of a central pacemaker in the brain's suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) and subsidiary clocks in nearly every body cell.

claims.text: Food-induced phase resetting proceeds faster in liver than in kidney, heart, or pancreas.
claims.quote: Food-induced phase resetting proceeds faster in liver than in kidney, heart, or pancreas, but after 1 wk of daytime feeding, the phases of circadian gene expression are similar in all examined peripheral tissues.

claims.text: Dysregulation of clock genes is linked to alterations in proliferation, metabolism, epithelial plasticity, immune regulation, metastatic potential, and treatment responsiveness in colorectal cancer.
claims.quote: statistically significant associations were consistently reported between dysregulation of clock genes such as PER1 , PER3 , CLOCK , BMAL1 , CRY1 , TIMELESS , and ARNTL2 and alterations in proliferation, metabolism, epithelial plasticity, immune regulation, metastatic potential, and treatment responsiveness.

verdict: The evidence confirms that circadian clocks are distributed throughout the body's tissues and can function independently of the central brain pacemaker.
caveat: The traditional hierarchical model is being replaced by a more integrated 'federated' model where local and systemic factors interact to regulate rhythms.
caption:
Your body is not a single machine directed by one clock.

Research shows that nearly every cell contains its own clock. These local rhythms can be adjusted independently by factors like food intake, creating a federated system rather than a simple hierarchy.

How does your daily routine affect your cells?
